Dermatology · published research

Alopecia areata

A small self-controlled study reported earlier regrowth in some irradiated patches. Case reports describe additional local regrowth, but durability and effects beyond limited patches remain uncertain.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A small self-controlled study reported earlier regrowth in some irradiated patches. Case reports describe additional local regrowth, but durability and effects beyond limited patches remain uncertain.

Summary of the Evidence

Six publications are mapped to alopecia areata: three primary human reports, one mouse experiment, one review, and one meta-analysis. The human evidence includes a self-controlled lesion study in 15 participants and two case reports. The meta-analysis combines laser or light treatment with topical minoxidil, so it does not estimate PBM monotherapy.

Human and clinical evidence

Yamazaki et al. studied 15 adults with patchy alopecia areata and compared 30 lesions within participants. Hair regrowth occurred earlier in seven of 15 irradiated areas than in the paired untreated areas, with a reported average difference of about 1.6 months. This design provides a direct comparison but remains small and lesion-based, and it does not establish long-term prevention of recurrence (Yamazaki et al. 2003). A later single-patient report described localized regrowth after daily 660 nm red-laser monotherapy, with follow-up over four months; an additional case described incidental focal regrowth during possible smartwatch light exposure. Neither case had a control group (Palma et al. 2023; Duncan and Tziotzios 2025).

Animal evidence

In C3H/HeJ mice, the Lexington LaserComb experiment reported hair regrowth by six weeks in treated animals while sham-treated animals did not regrow hair over that interval. This is one animal model and does not predict the size or durability of a response in people (Wikramanayake et al. 2012).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No separate indication-specific in-vitro or ex-vivo study was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The self-controlled study used a polarized broadband infrared source for intermittent three-minute exposure once weekly or every two weeks over about two months. The monotherapy case used continuous 660 nm visible red light daily for 21 days, while the mouse study used a 655 nm red-light comb. These are different devices and schedules. They do not establish a common dose, a preferred wavelength, or a treatment for widespread disease.

Interpretation

The lesion-level comparison reports earlier regrowth in some treated patches, and the case reports describe additional local observations. Because human evidence is small and alopecia areata can remit spontaneously, controlled replication is needed to determine the frequency, durability, and scope of any treatment effect.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for earlier regrowth in limited patchy alopecia areata Very low for durable or generalized regrowth
Publications and records6 articles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

One small self-controlled study compared treated and untreated patches in the same 15 people and found earlier regrowth in some treated areas. Two case reports and one mouse experiment add context, but hair loss can fluctuate and independent human replication is absent. A larger controlled study with standardized photographs and longer follow-up would clarify durability and which patients may respond.
